title: Business identity theft: how to spot a hijacked company
summary: Fraudsters can borrow the identity of a real company, including old and dormant ones, to get credit, open accounts or redirect payments.
body_markdown:
Business identity theft is when criminals pose as a real business, its owners or its officers to get cash, credit or loans in its name, leaving the business with the debts. It is also called corporate or commercial identity theft. A common form changes the company's record at the business registry, such as its address, officers or registered agent, and then uses the altered record to obtain loans or lines of credit.


They file changes to the company's public record at the business registry, such as a new address, new officers or a new registered agent, or file to reinstate a company that had been dissolved. In most US states the registry serves as the official place where business records are kept, and a filing that meets the basic requirements may be accepted without the registry questioning it or checking what it says. The fraudsters then add a lookalike email domain or website and use the company's name and history to apply for credit, order goods or open bank accounts.


Read the company's filing history for changes to its address, officers or registered agent made shortly before the application, or a reinstatement after years of inactivity. Check whether the new address, the new officer and the email domain connect to anything in the company's past, such as its archived website, directory listings and older filings. Then contact the company on a number you found yourself, from those older records, and ask for someone those records name.


An established company comes with a credit history, and a dormant one may have nobody checking its record. Colorado's Secretary of State says criminals "assume a business's identity and good credit history", and Texas's says they "target businesses that have been tax forfeited". The National Association of Secretaries of State lists unauthorised filings to reinstate a dissolved or inactive company among the forms of business hijacking.


Check your record and filing history at the registry, order a certified copy of any filing you did not make before you correct it, and tell the registry. Tell your bank, creditors and suppliers, ask whether they have seen recent or unusual charges or orders in your name, and report it to your local police. Online fraud can be reported to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, and in the UK fraud is reported to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland for a company registered in Scotland.


They can try, which is why registries offer protections. Thirteen of the 20 states that answered a survey reported in 2025 by the National Association of Secretaries of State offer an email or text alert when a filing is made on a company's record, and eleven have password protection or other verification for online filing. In the UK, Companies House's free Follow service emails you when a filing is accepted, and its PROOF scheme rejects paper versions of forms that change a company's registered office or officers.
